title: Cast-Iron Cornbread
wood: None — or 10 minutes on the pit after the oven
finish: Crackly crust, moist crumb, not cake
summary: Bacon fat in a screaming-hot skillet, cornmeal, buttermilk. The wedge you use to chase beans and greens.
story: Pit cornbread is not a yellow cake with a holiday name. It's a hot skillet, real cornmeal, buttermilk, and enough fat that the crust sounds like a crust. Sugar is a small argument — a teaspoon if the meal is bitter, more than that and you have made dessert. Pull it when the center just sets.

items: 2 Tbsp bacon fat or butter, for the pan
4 Tbsp melted butter or bacon fat

steps.title: Heat the iron
steps.body: Put a 10-inch skillet in a 425°F oven with the 2 Tbsp fat. It should shimmer, almost smoke, when you pull it.

steps.title: Batter, then pour
steps.body: Whisk dry. Whisk egg, buttermilk, melted fat. Combine without beating the life out of it. Pour into the hot skillet — it should hiss.

steps.title: Bake 18–22 minutes
steps.body: Golden, pulling from the sides, a toothpick with a few moist crumbs. Rest 5 minutes. Cut wedges. Butter on the table, not in the batter.

proTips.text: If the crust isn't brown you didn't heat the skillet. The oven time is easy. The hiss is the recipe.

milestones.label: Bake
milestones.hint: Hiss when it hits. Golden, 18–22 minutes.

title: Memphis BBQ Spaghetti
finish: Noodles stained red, pork in every forkful
summary: Spaghetti, pulled pork, and a thin tomato-barbecue gravy. The Memphis side that confuses everyone who isn't from Memphis.
story: The Bar-B-Q Shop and a handful of other Memphis joints serve spaghetti like it's the most obvious thing in the world: leftover pork, a tomato-mustard sauce, noodles that aren't al dente on purpose. It is not Italian. It is a starch that drinks sauce the way white bread does, except it stays on the plate. Make it with chopped pork shoulder and the Memphis wet, thinned.

items: 2 cups Memphis wet sauce (or a thin tomato-mustard barbecue sauce)
1 cup pork drippings, stock, or water
1 tsp kosher salt, plus pasta water salt

steps.title: Build a thin gravy
steps.body: Sweat onion and garlic in fat. Add sauce and stock. Simmer 10 minutes until it tastes like barbecue and still pours. Fold in the pork.

steps.title: Soft noodles
steps.body: Boil spaghetti past al dente — Memphis wants it stained and a little soft. Drain, save a splash of pasta water.

steps.title: Toss like you mean it
steps.body: Noodles into the gravy. Loosen with pasta water if it clutches. The pork should be in every bite, not a garnish. Plate in a bowl. Extra sauce on the side.

proTips.text: If you serve this with Parmesan a pitmaster from Cleveland Street will come to your house. Hot sauce, maybe. Cheese, no.

milestones.label: Thin pork gravy
milestones.hint: Sauce plus stock, pork folded in.

milestones.label: Stain the noodles
milestones.hint: Past al dente. Pork in every fork.

title: Pit Banana Pudding
pitTemp: None — or a torch for the meringue
finish: Set custard, bananas still pale, wafers softened but not mush
summary: From-scratch vanilla pudding, Nilla wafers, bananas. The closer every pit plate in the South already agreed on.
story: Banana pudding is not a side in the USDA sense. It is the thing you eat standing up after the brisket, out of a hotel pan, with a wafer that has gone soft on purpose. Cook a real vanilla custard. Layer. Rest. Meringue if you are showing off, whipped cream if you are not. Box pudding is a weeknight confession, not a pitmaster recipe.

items: Meringue: 4 egg whites + ¼ cup sugar, or 1½ cups whipped cream

steps.title: Cook the custard
steps.body: Whisk sugar, flour, salt in a saucepan. Stream in milk. Cook over medium, whisking, until thick. Temper yolks, return to the pot 2 minutes. Off heat: butter, vanilla. It should coat a spoon.

steps.title: Layer
steps.body: Wafers, bananas, custard, repeat in a 9×13 or a deep bowl. End with custard. Don't use brown bananas — they'll go to slime by tomorrow.

steps.title: Top and rest
steps.body: Meringue browned under a broiler or whipped cream. Fridge at least 2 hours so the wafers soften. Serve cold with a big spoon.

proTips.text: The wafers are supposed to go limp. If they're still crisp you plated too soon. If the bananas are brown you waited too long. There is a window. Hit it.

milestones.label: Custard thick
milestones.hint: Coats a spoon. Vanilla off heat.

milestones.label: Layer and rest
milestones.hint: Wafers, banana, pudding. Two hours cold.

title: Potlikker Collards
finish: Silky leaves, pot liquor worth a cornbread dunk
summary: Greens, a smoked hog jowl or hock, vinegar at the end. The Carolina pot that makes the meat look lonely without it.
story: Collards are a time dish. Strip the stems, simmer with a smoked hock until the leaves go from bicycle-tire to silk, and don't you dare throw out the pot liquor. Vinegar and hot sauce at the table. Cornbread is the utensil. These are not a garnish of steamed baby kale.

items: 2 bunches collard greens (about 2 lb), stems stripped, leaves chopped
1 smoked ham hock or 6 oz hog jowl
2 Tbsp cider vinegar at the end

steps.title: Wash like you mean it
steps.body: Collards hide grit. Two or three cold-water baths until the sink is clean.

steps.title: Hock first
steps.body: Simmer hock, onion, garlic, stock 45 minutes. Add greens, packed down, salt, peppers. They will collapse.

steps.title: Low and long
steps.body: Bare simmer 90 minutes to 2 hours until the leaves are silky and the hock is shreddable. Pull meat from the bone, return it. Vinegar. Taste the liquor — more salt if it's shy.

proTips.text: The liquor is the dish. If you drain the greens you have made a wet salad and wasted a hock.

milestones.label: Silky leaves
milestones.hint: 90+ minutes. Hock shredded back in. Vinegar.

title: Hush Puppies
finish: Crackly, onion-sweet, steam when you break one
summary: Cornmeal batter, onion, a hot pot of oil. The Carolina crunch that shows up next to whole hog whether you asked or not.
story: Hush puppies are a fry-house side that barbecue borrowed and kept. Onion in the batter, a little sugar if the meal is harsh, dropped by the spoon into 350°F oil until they roll themselves over. They should be done in the middle without going greasy. Salt them the second they leave the pot.

items: ½ small onion, minced, or 3 scallions

steps.title: Batter rest
steps.body: Whisk dry. Whisk buttermilk and egg, fold in with onion. Rest 10 minutes while the oil heats to 350–365°F. Batter should plop, not pour.

steps.title: Drop and roll
steps.body: Heaping tablespoons, 5–6 at a time. Don't crowd. 2–3 minutes until deep gold, turning as they bob. Drain on a rack. Salt immediately.

proTips.text: If they're raw in the middle your oil was too hot. If they're greasy it was too cool. 350°F is the job. A thermometer, not a vibe.

title: Smoked Creamed Corn
finish: Creamy, a few charred kernels, black pepper on top
summary: Fresh corn, cream, a cast-iron pan on the pit. Kansas City sweetness without turning the side into candy.
story: Creamed corn on a smoker is a 40-minute job if you don't drown it in sugar. Cut the kernels, scrape the milk from the cobs, fold in cream and a little butter, and let the pan pick up a hint of apple wood. Frozen corn works in January. A teaspoon of sugar is plenty if the ears were dull.

items: 6 ears corn, kernels cut, cobs scraped (or 6 cups frozen, thawed)
1 tsp sugar, only if the corn is shy

steps.title: Sweat the onion
steps.body: Butter, onion, 3 minutes in a 10-inch skillet. Add corn and cob scrapings. Salt, pepper, paprika.

steps.title: Cream, then smoke
steps.body: Stir in cream and milk. Set the skillet on the pit at 275°F, 35–45 minutes, stirring the edges once, until it thickens and a few kernels take color. Taste. Sugar only if needed.

proTips.text: Hickory plus cream plus sugar is how you make a candle. Apple wood, and stop stirring so the top can take a little bark.

milestones.label: Skillet on the pit
milestones.hint: 275°F until creamy with a few charred bits.

title: Santa Maria Pinquito Beans
wood: Red oak if they're finishing on the pit
finish: Small pink beans in a savory broth, not molasses
summary: Pinquitos, bacon, chile. The Central Coast pot that sits next to tri-tip instead of sweet pit beans.
story: Santa Maria barbecue is tri-tip, red oak, salsa, and a pot of pinquito beans — a small pink bean grown in the valley that doesn't taste like Kansas City. Bacon, onion, tomato, a little chile. No molasses. If you cannot find pinquitos, small pink beans or a mix of pinto and white will get you close. The broth should be spoonable, not candy.

items: 1 lb pinquito beans, soaked overnight (or small pink beans)
4 oz bacon or salt pork, diced
1 Tbsp chile powder or 1 minced jalapeño
Water or stock to cover by 2 inches

steps.title: Render and sweat
steps.body: Bacon until it gives up fat. Onion and garlic in that fat. Tomato, chile, mustard, bay.

steps.title: Simmer the beans
steps.body: Drained beans, cover with water. Gentle simmer until tender, 90 minutes to 2 hours. Salt in the last 30 so the skins don't toughen. Add water if they drink it.

steps.title: Optional smoke finish
steps.body: Uncovered on the pit 30 minutes next to the tri-tip if you want a hint of oak. Serve in a bowl with the liquor. Salsa on the meat, beans on the side.

proTips.text: These are not pit beans with a California sticker. If you add molasses you have left Santa Maria.

title: Alabama Cheese Grits
finish: Spoonable, cheddar melted, black pepper on top
summary: Stone-ground grits, cheddar, a little cream. The Alabama bowl under smoked chicken and white sauce.
story: If you put white sauce on a bird, the starch underneath should be grits, not a roll. Stone-ground if you can find them — they take 30–40 minutes and taste like corn instead of wallpaper paste. Cheddar at the end, not out of a packet. A pat of butter. Pepper. Leftovers set up and fry like polenta the next morning, which is a gift.

items: ¼ cup cream or a splash more milk
Optional: dash of hot sauce or Worcestershire

steps.title: Whisk into simmering liquid
steps.body: Water, milk, salt to a simmer. Rain the grits in, whisking so they don't clump. Drop to low.

steps.title: Slow and stirred
steps.body: 25–40 minutes depending on the grind, stirring often, until creamy and the raw-corn bite is gone. Add a splash of water if they seize.

steps.title: Cheese off heat
steps.body: Butter, cheddar, cream. Pepper. They should ribbon off a spoon. Hold on low, loosen with milk as they sit.

proTips.text: Instant grits are a different food. If that's what you have, don't invite anyone from Birmingham.

title: Pit Pimento Cheese
finish: Spreadable, pimentos visible, sharp cheddar in the nose
summary: Grated cheddar, pimentos, a little mayo. The Alabama/Georgia spread that belongs on celery, saltines, and a leftover brisket sandwich.
story: Pimento cheese is a side, a starter, and a condiment depending on how hungry the pit is. Grate the cheese yourself. Drain the pimentos. Mayo, a little pickle brine or Worcestershire, cayenne. It should look like cheese with pimentos, not a pink dip. Make it a few hours ahead.

items: 4 oz extra-sharp white cheddar or Monterey Jack, grated
1 (4 oz) jar pimentos, drained and chopped
1 tsp pickle brine or cider vinegar
¼ tsp cayenne or hot sauce

steps.title: Don't use the food processor
steps.body: A processor turns this into paste. Fold mayo, brine, Worcestershire, salt, pepper, cayenne. Add cheese and pimentos. It should be clumpy-spreadable.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Cover, fridge 1 hour. Serve with saltines, celery, or on white bread. A smear on a brisket sandwich is not traditional and is also correct.

proTips.text: Pre-shredded cheddar is coated in starch and tastes like the bag. Grate it. That is the entire standard of quality.

milestones.label: Cold rest
milestones.hint: An hour. Crackers, celery, leftover meat.

title: Hatch Street Corn
wood: Mesquite or whatever is in the fire
summary: Corn on the cob, charred, then crema, cotija, Hatch chile. The Southwest cob that stands in for coleslaw.
story: Elote showed up at barbecue because lime and chile do what vinegar slaw does — cut fat — with fire already going. Char the ears over the hot side, slather, roll in cotija, dust with chile. Off the cob in a bowl (esquites) if you are feeding a crowd with plates instead of fists.

items: ½ cup Mexican crema or sour cream thinned with lime
2 tsp Hatch or New Mexico chile powder

steps.title: Char the ears
steps.body: Oil, hot grate, turn until blistered all over, 8–12 minutes. A little black is flavor. All black is ash.

steps.title: Slather and roll
steps.body: Mix crema and mayo. Paint the hot ears, roll in cotija, dust chile, salt, cilantro. Lime at the table. For a bowl: cut kernels, toss with the same dressing.

proTips.text: Tajín is fine. Chili powder from a taco packet is cumin and regret. Use chile that is actually chile.

title: Cajun Dirty Rice
finish: Rice stained brown, liver in the background not the foreground
summary: Rice, chicken liver, sausage, the holy trinity. The Louisiana plate under smoked turkey and a butter mop.
story: Dirty rice is supposed to look like it worked for a living. Chicken liver and sausage brown until they almost catch, trinity in that fat, rice that drinks stock. The liver should be a rumor, not a punch. If you skip it you have made rice dressing's shy cousin. Serve next to a Cajun-rubbed bird, not as a bed for brisket.

items: 8 oz chicken livers, trimmed and minced
8 oz Cajun sausage or andouille, small dice
1 tsp Cajun pit rub or paprika plus cayenne

steps.title: Brown past polite
steps.body: Oil, sausage, then liver, high heat, until browned and the pan has bits. That's the dirt. Don't steam them in a crowded pan — work in batches if you have to.

steps.title: Trinity, then rice
steps.body: Onion, pepper, celery in the fat until soft. Garlic a minute. Rice, toast 1 minute. Stock, rub, salt, bay. Bring to a boil, lid, low 18 minutes.

steps.title: Rest and scallion
steps.body: Off heat 10 minutes, lid on. Fork through. Scallions. Taste for cayenne. It should be savory and a little muddy, not tomato-red.

proTips.text: If you can't taste liver at all you were shy. If that's all you taste you didn't brown the sausage first. The order is the recipe.

milestones.label: Liver and sausage brown
milestones.hint: Fond in the pan. That's the dirt.

title: Preston's Peach Cobbler
wood: Pecan or peach, or none — oven 375°F
pitTemp: 375°F oven or a 350°F pit, away from the firebox
finish: Biscuit brown, filling bubbling at the edge
summary: Peak peaches, a drop-biscuit lid, cast iron. The cobbler that can ride the pit while the pork rests.
story: Peach cobbler is not pie and it is not dump cake. Fruit goes in a hot skillet with sugar, lemon, a little cornstarch. Biscuit dough gets dropped on top so steam can still get out. Bake until the lid is brown and the juice is a syrup, not soup. Fresh peaches in season. Frozen in January — thawed and drained, no apology. Ice cream is not optional.

items: 6 cups sliced peaches (about 3 lb), peeled if the skins bother you
2 Tbsp sugar, plus more to dust
½ cup cold buttermilk, plus a splash

steps.body: 12-inch cast iron. Toss peaches with sugar, cornstarch, lemon, cinnamon, salt. Butter in the pan, fruit in, medium heat 5 minutes until it looks juicy. If you're using the pit, do this on the stove then move the skillet over.
steps.title: Heat the fruit

steps.body: Flour, sugar, baking powder, salt. Cut in butter to peas. Stir buttermilk just until it comes together. Drop 8 spoonfuls on the fruit. Dust sugar.
steps.title: Drop the lid

steps.body: 375°F oven 30–40 minutes, or 350°F pit away from the firebox 40–50, until biscuits are brown and the edge is bubbling. Rest 15 minutes so you don't napalm a mouth. Ice cream on the plate, not in the pan.
steps.title: Bake until it talks

proTips.text: If the filling is watery you skipped the cornstarch or you used hard winter peaches. Frozen fruit has more water — drain it or add another teaspoon of starch.

milestones.hint: Juicy in the skillet, not soupy.
milestones.label: Fruit hot

milestones.hint: Dropped, not rolled. Sugar on top.
milestones.label: Biscuit lid
